newsitem.title: MEXICO: Suspected Mexican rebels arrested in Chiapas state.
newsitem.headline: Suspected Mexican rebels arrested in Chiapas state.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-11-27

text.p: Two suspected members of a Mexican rebel group were found carrying a portable rocket laucher and have been arrested, officials said on Wednesday.

The state attorney general's office said in a report the presumed members of the new Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) were found camped in the mountains in the troubled southern state of Chiapas with a Russian-made RPG anti-tank missile launcher and three 70 mm anti-tank missiles.
The two men, identified as peasant farmers Cristobal Garcia and Albino Castro, were discovered on Nov. 16 in the town of Motozintla on the Mexico-Guatemala border.

The report said the men confessed to being EPR members and buying the missile launcher on the Central American black market for about $5,000 plus $125 to have the weapon smuggled across the border through unknown middlemen.
But the two, jailed in the Chiapas capital of Tuxtla Gutierrez, have denied the charges and said they confessed only after being tortured, the local newspaper Este Sur said.
Chiapas government undersecretary Uriel Jarquin confirmed the arrest in a telephone interview with Reuters but declined to offer further details on the charges.

"It is a weapon to destroy vehicles. It is very dangerous," Gen. Mario Renan Castillo told Este Sur. He said the RPG missile launcher could be "the most important weapon" seized in Chiapas since Jan. 1, 1994, when a separate guerrilla group, the Zapatista National Liberation Army, launched a bloody uprising.

The fighting ended after a few days and the Zapatistas have been involved in peace talks with the government for nearly two years. Zapatista leader Subcommandante Marcos has denied any link with the EPR, which emerged in June in the mountains of another of Mexico's poorest regions, the southwestern state of Guerrero.
Since June the EPR has launched scattered surprise attacks in at least four Mexican states.
